thread.title_full: U.S. Forest Service builds 'bat condo' near Clackamas Lake - NewsBreak

author: Christopher Keizur
title: U.S. Forest Service builds 'bat condo' near Clackamas Lake - NewsBreak
text:
By Christopher Keizur ,
1 days ago
About 100 little brown bats were found roosting in the shutters of the Clackamas Lake Guard Station, a historic cabin seasonally open to the public for recreation rentals.
When mulling how to encourage those critters to find a new place to sleep — and prevent the cabin from transforming into Bruce Wayne’s Batcave — U.S. Forest Service wildlife biologists came up with a plan.
So, in honor of National Bat Week (Oct. 24-31), a special “bat condo” was built. The new bat house offers a large, purpose-built roosting location while protecting the 1933 cabin.
The project began with consultations with botanists, biologists, and archaeologists to review the proposed bat condo site and installation procedures, ensuring no damage near the lake. Forest staff then used fees collected from commercial filing permits to purchase the bat condo and installation supplies.
Alaska Recreational Management provided labor to install the condo near the cabin.
“This collaborative project is a win for helping these bats thrive while protecting our historic buildings in the forest,” the U.S. Forest Service wrote.
A few bats have already moved into their new home. Wildlife experts expect more to arrive in the spring, when female little brown bats form large maternity colonies, roosting to give birth and raise their pups.
Little Brown Bats
The little brown bat has a widespread range in North America, from the Alaska-Canada boreal forests south through most of the contiguous United States and into central Mexico.
The species was once abundant but has declined sharply, especially in the east, due to white-nose syndrome, a fungal disease.
They love to eat all sorts of insects, from mosquitoes and moths to small beetles and spiders.
Clackamas Lake Historic House
The 1,380-square-foot, two-story cabin is off Oregon Skyline Road, near Clackamas Lake and its campground. The cabin has a knotty pine interior and exterior that resembles a log cabin in the Cascadian style.
It once served as the district ranger’s home base. It was built in 1933 by the Civilian Conservation Corps and is across the road from the old District Ranger’s Office (now a visitor center).
